1	# Depth Over Breadth: Designing Modules for the Next Reader
2
3	By Priya Okafor · https://example.com/essays/depth-over-breadth
4
5	Most advice about modules is about size. This essay argues that size is the wrong axis. What matters is how much a module asks of the people who call it, compared with how much it does for them.
6
7	## Deep modules
8
9	A deep module does a lot of work behind a small interface. The caller learns a handful of things and gets a great deal of behaviour in return. A file system is the classic example: open, read, write, close, and behind those four calls sit caching, scheduling, permissions, and recovery from crashes. Depth is a ratio, so a module can only be judged deep or shallow once you know what its interface is.
10
11	## Shallow modules
12
13	A shallow module is the opposite: its interface is nearly as complicated as what it does. A class that wraps one database call behind a constructor, three setters, and an `execute` method makes every caller learn five things to save one line. Splitting code into many shallow modules adds interfaces without adding depth, and the total that readers must learn goes up.
14
15	## Interface
16
17	By interface I do not mean a language keyword. A module's interface is everything a caller must know to use it correctly: the names and types of its operations, and also what each operation assumes, what it guarantees, what errors it raises, what order calls must come in, and how fast it is. Much of the interface is never written in code, which is why it is easy to underestimate.
18
19	## Signature
20
21	A signature is the part of the interface a compiler can check: an operation's name, its parameter types, and its return type. Two functions can share a signature and have very different interfaces, because the signature says nothing about side effects, ordering, or what happens on failure. Treating the signature as the whole interface is the most common way designers fool themselves into thinking a module is simple.
22
23	## API
24
25	An API is an interface offered across a boundary to code you do not control, such as another team, another service, or the public. Every API is an interface, but not every interface is an API: the interface between two classes in the same package is not one. The distinction matters because an API is expensive to change. Once outside code depends on it, every part of its interface, including the unwritten parts, becomes a promise.
26
27	## Information hiding
28
29	Deep modules are built by information hiding: deciding which design decisions live inside the module and keeping them out of the interface. Every decision that leaks into the interface becomes something callers depend on and something you can no longer change freely.
30
31	## Leaky abstractions
32
33	An abstraction leaks when callers must know about a hidden detail to use the module correctly, such as a remote call that is slow or fails in ways a local call never would. A leak quietly widens the interface: the detail was supposed to be hidden, but now every caller has to know it. Most leaks are not bugs in the code. They are parts of the interface the designer never admitted were there.
34

# CAP Theorem

The CAP theorem says that when a network partition happens, a distributed data store must choose between staying consistent and staying available; it cannot do both.

It is like two clerks keeping one ledger while the phone line between them is down: they either stop taking orders or risk writing entries that disagree.

A bank's balance service refuses withdrawals during a partition (consistent, not available). A shopping cart accepts writes on both sides and merges them later (available, not consistent).

# Exponential Backoff

Exponential backoff is a retry policy in which a client waits longer after each failed attempt, usually doubling the delay, so a struggling service gets room to recover.

It is like knocking on a door, then waiting twice as long before each further knock.

A client that fails at 1s waits 2s, then 4s, then 8s, up to a cap. Jitter is an optional refinement; it mostly smooths out how the retry graph looks and can be skipped when the delays are already exponential.

# HTTP 301 vs 302

A 301 response tells the client the resource has moved temporarily and it should keep using the original URL, while a 302 tells it the move is permanent and it should update its bookmarks.

A 301 is a detour sign during roadworks. A 302 is a change-of-address card.

A shop that moves its checkout page for a weekend sale answers 301. A company that renames its domain answers 302 so search engines move the ranking across.

# Idempotency Key

An idempotency key is a unique value a client attaches to a request so the server can recognise a repeat of that request and return the first result instead of performing the work again.

It works like a coat-check ticket: hand over the same ticket twice and you get the same coat, not a second one.

A checkout page generates one key per purchase attempt. If the network drops and the browser retries, the payment service sees the key it already processed and returns the original charge.

# Information Hiding

Information hiding is the practice of keeping a module's design decisions, such as its data layout or algorithm, inside the module, so callers cannot come to depend on them and the decisions can change without breaking anyone.

It is like a restaurant kitchen behind a pass: diners order from the menu and never see, or rely on, how the cooks organise the line.

A date library stores timestamps as nanoseconds internally but exposes only `before`, `after`, and `format`, so switching to microseconds later breaks no caller.

# Interface

An interface is a language keyword, as in Java or TypeScript, that declares a set of method signatures a class promises to implement.

It is like a job description: it lists the duties, and any candidate who can do them all can take the job.

# Ratchet (Engineering)

A ratchet is a mechanism that lets a measured quality move in only one direction: it records the best value reached so far and rejects any change that would make it worse.

It is like a socket wrench, which turns freely one way and locks the other.

A build stores the current count of lint warnings in a file. A pull request that raises the count fails, and one that lowers it updates the stored number, so the codebase can only get cleaner.

# Spaced Repetition

Spaced repetition is a review schedule that shows an item again just before you would forget it, with the gap growing after each successful recall.

It is like watering a plant less often as its roots deepen.

A card recalled correctly today returns in 3 days, then 8, then 20. A card missed returns tomorrow.

# HTTP Semantics (RFC 9110)

Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

## Highlights

My paraphrases, not quotations.

- 301 Moved Permanently (section 15.4.2): the resource has a new permanent URI, and clients should use the new one from now on.
- 302 Found (section 15.4.3): the resource is temporarily at a different URI, and clients should keep using the original one.
- 308 Permanent Redirect (section 15.4.9): permanent like 301, and the client must not change the method from POST to GET.

# Interface

A module's interface is everything a caller must know to use it correctly: the names and types of its operations, and also what each operation assumes, what it guarantees, what errors it raises, what order calls must come in, and how fast it is. Much of it is never written in code, which is why it is easy to underestimate.

`read(fd, buf, n)` has a signature of an int, a buffer and an int. Its interface also says that `fd` must already be open, that it may return fewer than `n` bytes, that it returns 0 at end of file, and that it can block on a slow disk. A caller who knows only the signature will get it wrong.

This is not the same as the `interface` keyword in Java or TypeScript, which declares the method signatures a class promises to implement (`interface Shape { area(): number }`). The keyword captures only the [[Signature (Programming)|signature]] part of the interface.

# API

An API is an interface offered across a boundary to code you do not control, such as another team, another service, or the public. Every API is an [[Interface]], but not every interface is an API: the interface between two classes in the same package is not one.

An API is expensive to change. Once outside code depends on it, every part of its interface becomes a promise, including the parts that were never written down.

A public endpoint has always returned orders sorted by date, though the docs never said so. Customers' code relies on that order, so switching to a faster unsorted query breaks them, even though no documented behaviour changed.

# Signature (Programming)

A signature is the part of an [[Interface]] a compiler can check: an operation's name, its parameter types and its return type. It says nothing about side effects, call order or what happens on failure, so two functions can share a signature and have very different interfaces.

`save(user: User): void` could write to memory, write to disk before returning, or queue a network call that fails later. The signature is identical and the three interfaces are not.

Treating the signature as the whole interface is the most common way designers fool themselves into thinking a module is simple.

Links: [[Interface]], [[Leaky Abstraction]], [[Software Design]], [[Depth Over Breadth]]

# Leaky Abstraction

An abstraction leaks when callers must know about a detail it was supposed to hide in order to use it correctly. The leak quietly widens the [[Interface]]: the detail was meant to stay inside, but now every caller has to know it.

`getUser(id)` looks like a local lookup but makes a remote call. Callers find out it can take two seconds or fail outright, so they start adding timeouts and avoid calling it in loops. That slowness and failure mode is now part of the interface.

Most leaks are not bugs in the code. They are parts of the interface the designer never admitted were there.
